`cuda_graphs.modules_of(model)` lists them. Use the census to get the path instead of writing it by hand:

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import cuda_graphs

census_user = cuda_graphs.Census(cuda_graphs.modules_of(model_user))
for _ in range(3):
    model_user(observation_user)
    census_user.end_act()
census_user.close()
print(census_user.candidates())        # [{'path': 'denoiser', 'calls': 10, 'ms': 1.05}]
```

The line is printed on a machine with no GPU too, so a mistyped path shows up on a laptop.

### `cuda graphs: ... is not a torch module: not captured`

The path names something that is not a `torch.nn.Module`: a function, a tensor, a list. Name the module that contains
it.

### `cuda graphs: ... runs in eager mode for one of its shapes: ...`

One shape of that module's inputs could not be graphed, and runs in eager mode from now on. The other shapes are
unaffected. The text after the colon gives the reason:

- `its capture failed (...)`: the module does something a CUDA graph cannot record, with torch's own error in
  parentheses. Naming a smaller module inside it often works.
- `its output is of a type a graph cannot return`: the module returns something other than tensors and plain
  values.
- `its graph's output differed from eager mode's`: the replay did not equal eager mode byte for byte, so it is not used.
  The check is working as intended, and that shape stays in eager mode.
- `cuda graphs need torch 2.4 or later`: older torch cannot swap the GPU's random generator while a capture runs,
  and a failed capture would corrupt your model's random noise. Nothing is captured. Upgrade torch.

### I installed it and nothing got faster

In order of likelihood:

1. **The module is called once per run.** The gain comes from the kernel launches across many calls. Run the census:
   `calls` is the number of calls per run.
2. **The model was not launch-bound.** A model whose GPU is already busy nearly all the time has no launch overhead
   to remove: π0.5 under JAX was 98% GPU-busy.
3. **Every call has a new shape.** Each new shape is captured once; a run of new shapes is a run of captures.
4. **It is running in eager mode.** Look for a `runs in eager mode` line above.

[How do I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its outputs?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)

## `batcher`

### `ValueError: sizes [2, 4] must include 1: a call that waits alone is a batch of 1, and a batch in which the model raised is re-run call by call`

Include 1 in the sizes: `Batcher(run, sizes=[1, 2, 4])`. A call that arrives alone must be dispatched as a batch of
one.

### `ValueError: the model returned 3 outputs for a batch of 4`

Your function must return one output for each input, in order. It is given a list and returns a list of the same
length.

### My batches are all of size 1

Calls are batched only while they wait. With an idle model and `wait_ms=0`, each call is dispatched as soon as it
arrives. Raise `wait_ms` slightly (the examples use 2 ms), or expect batches only when the model is busy.

## `replicas`

### `TypeError: load must be a function a new process can import: defined at a module's top level, not a lambda and not a function inside another`

Each replica starts in its own process and imports `load_user` by name. Move it to the top of a module:

```python
def load_user():                       # at the top of a module, not inside main() and not a lambda
    model_user = build_model_user()
    return model_user.infer            # what one call runs
```

### `ReplicaStartFailed: the model's load raised: ...`

Your `load_user` raised in the replica's process; the text after the colon is its error, and the exception's `traceback`
is the replica's. Run `load()` once in a plain script to see it directly.

### `ReplicaStartFailed: the model did not load within 900 s`

The replica did not finish loading in time. For a model that takes longer: `ReplicaPool(load, start_timeout=1800)`.

### `ReplicaDied: the replica died mid-call (exit code -9)`

The process has exited: killed, or out of memory (an exit code of -9 is SIGKILL, which is also what the Linux
out-of-memory killer sends). The pool replaces it, and the call that was running gets this error. `ReplicaError`, by
contrast, is your model's own exception: the replica is alive and takes the next call.

### `ReplicaDied: the call exceeded its ... s deadline: the replica was terminated`

A call took longer than the deadline you gave it. The replica is terminated and replaced, since a model stuck in a call
cannot be interrupted any other way.

### `PoolHalted: ...`

The pool stopped replacing replicas after three consecutive deaths (`deaths_in_a_row`), or it was closed; the text
after the colon states which. A model that dies on every call is not reloaded indefinitely. Fix the cause, and create
a new pool.

### `ValueError: 1 replicas and 2 devices: one device per replica, at least one replica`

`devices` has one entry for each replica: `ReplicaPool(load, replicas=2, devices=[0, 1])`.

### Two replicas on one GPU are no faster

That is what was measured:
[Should I run two replicas of a policy on one GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/should-i-run-two-replicas-of-a-policy-on-one-gpu.md)

## `slack`

### `SizeFailed`

`slack.measure` could not run your forward pass at one of the batch sizes you listed, for example a batch that does
not fit in GPU memory. The exception carries the size, the timings measured so far, and your forward pass's own
error. List only the sizes that run.

### A replica serves only one robot

The policy leaves no slack: its robot requests the next chunk only when the current one is fully executed, so there
is no time in which to wait for a batch. See "Rules and requirements" in [`docs/slack.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/slack.md#rules-and-requirements).

## General

### Does any of this change my policy's outputs?

No. `cuda_graphs` keeps a graph only when its output equals eager mode's byte for byte. `batcher` returns to each
call the output your model produced for it. `replicas` and `slack` do not modify the model. No network component
touches the model, and `compress` is lossless: the server gets back the bytes the robot built.
`frames.resize_image` and `frames.encode` do change pixels, which is their purpose, and only where you call them: the
resize mode and filter have no default, so you name the ones your policy was trained with. `openpi.image_tools` resizes
as openpi's own does and then sends JPEG, and a server started through `sequence_ai.network.openpi` hands the policy the
JPEG's pixels: at quality 95 they moved a π0.5 policy's actions by 5.9% on average over 50 real observations, about a
tenth of what the policy's own sampling noise moves them.

### Do I need a GPU to try it?

No. The tests and every example except `examples/check_on_a_gpu.py` run on a machine with no GPU.

### Does it work on Windows?

It is tested on Linux and macOS. `replicas` starts its processes with `spawn`, which is available on all three, but
nothing here is tested on Windows.

### Something else

Open an issue at <https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/issues> with a minimal script that reproduces it,
the full error text and the output of `python -c "import sys, platform; print(sys.version, platform.platform())"`.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md

# How do I get a GPU near my robot?

Use any GPU the robot can reach: one you own, one from a cloud provider, or one rented near the robot. Whichever it is,
the robot's code changes in one line, the address it connects to, and the components in this repository are used on
that GPU in the same way.

```python
import sequence_ai

link_user = sequence_ai.connect("http://ADDRESS:8000")       # the GPU's address
```

GPUs are in short supply, and few are near any given robot. [General Sequences](https://generalsequences.com) rents
them by location, with this package's `seq gpu` commands: you name a city, a GPU is started near it, and you have root
in a container on it.

```bash
seq gpu places san fr                                           # the US cities a place can be
seq gpu add --place "San Francisco, CA" --gpu L4 --port 8000    # one GPU near it, and the port your server listens on
seq gpu ssh <id>                                                # root in its container: start your policy server
seq gpu remove <id>                                             # ends it, and its disk with it
```

The port is open to the address `seq gpu add` was run from; `seq gpu allow <id> <the robot's address>` opens it to the
robot, an IPv6 range as well as an IPv4 one. A robot whose address changes, on a cellular or satellite line, gets a
follow token, `seq gpu follow-token <id> --robot <name>`, and connects with `sequence_ai.connect(url, follow=token)`
(or `$SEQUENCES_FOLLOW_TOKEN` set): its address of the moment is let in before it connects, and with two uplinks
(`lines=["eth0", "wwan0"]`) each line's, by a follow that goes out by that line. Over IPv4, a cellular or satellite
line's public address is usually shared by many of its provider's customers (carrier-grade NAT), and letting that
address in lets them all in: where `seq gpu list` shows the GPU an IPv6 address, connect to that address or to the
GPU's name, so that the robot follows over IPv6, and start the server with a token either way.

This is a paid service, billed while the GPU runs. Everything else on this page, and every component, works the same on
any other GPU. [Its documentation](https://generalsequences.com/docs/gpus/) has the rest.

## Why near

A robot that requests its next actions from a remote GPU waits for the model and for the network, and the network's
share grows with distance. The inference layer (`sequence_ai.engine`) reduces the model's time, the network layer
(`sequence_ai.network`) removes round trips the connection does not need, and the distance itself depends on where the
GPU is.

## The same line, for each client

| Your robot uses | The line that changes |
|---|---|
| `sequence_ai.network.connect()` | `connect("http://ADDRESS:8000")` |
| The quickstart's robot | `python quickstart_robot.py http://ADDRESS:8000` |
| openpi's client | `WebsocketClientPolicy(host="ADDRESS", port=8000)` |
| LeRobot's remote inference | its `endpoint`, `tcp/ADDRESS:PORT` |

The inference components need no change on a new GPU:

```bash
pip install sequence-ai
python examples/check_on_a_gpu.py        # the capture, checked against eager mode on that GPU
```

## Before the robot connects

- **The server listens on every address.** `127.0.0.1` is reachable from the GPU itself only. `serve()` listens on
  every address unless it is given `host`: `python quickstart_server.py` does.
- **The port is open to the robot.** A rented GPU's firewall usually admits no one until you open a port. Open the
  server's port to the address or range the robot connects from, or follow the robot's address with `follow=`. If you
  open it to everyone, start the server with a token: `serve(policy, token="...")`, and `connect(url, token="...")` on
  the robot.

## Then measure

A GPU nearer the robot shortens the RTT, and the network components remove round trips that are not needed at all.
Which of them help on the new link is something to measure:
[How do I measure the link between my robot and my GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md)
The measuring tool's server listens on port 9000 by default, so open that port too.

## Tested

The client side was tested against a server at another address of the same machine:
`python quickstart_robot.py http://ADDRESS:8017` printed its three requests.

## See also

- [How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md)
- [How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)
- [How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md)

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-keep-a-websocket-policy-servers-connection-warm.md

# How do I keep a WebSocket policy server's connection warm?

Have the server ping each connection every 100 ms. A WebSocket library answers a ping with a pong by itself, so a
server that pings makes the robot send a few bytes each interval, and the robot's kernel never counts the connection
as idle. Nothing changes on the robot: not its program, and not its library.

With the `websockets` library:

```python
import websockets
from sequence_ai.network import ping

# websockets' own server, with a ping every 100 ms
async with ping.serve(handler_user, host_user, port_user) as server_user:
    await server_user.serve_forever()

# the same, as its options
async with websockets.serve(handler_user, host_user, port_user, **ping.websockets_options()):
    ...
```

openpi's own policy server is built on the `websockets` library. Started through `python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi`,
it pings each connection the same way, with no change to its files:
[How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)

Under uvicorn:

```python
import uvicorn
from sequence_ai.network import ping

uvicorn.run(app_user, **ping.uvicorn_options())
```

```bash
pip install sequence-ai          # this component imports only the standard library, and websockets for ping.serve
```

`ping.websockets_options()` and `ping.uvicorn_options()` return plain options, so you can also write them out and
install nothing:

```text
ping.websockets_options()  ->  {'ping_interval': 0.1, 'ping_timeout': 20.0}
ping.uvicorn_options()     ->  {'ws_ping_interval': 0.1, 'ws_ping_timeout': 20.0}
```

Without them, `websockets` pings every 20 seconds (the default of its `serve` in version 17.4). That finds a dead
connection. It is far too slow to keep a connection from going idle between a robot's requests.

## Why it matters

On Linux, a connection that has sent nothing for longer than its retransmission timeout has its congestion window
restarted, so the robot's next observation can take more round trips to upload. What restarts it is the robot's own
silence, which is why a ping the robot must answer fixes it from the server side.
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
mechanism in full.

## Try it

[`examples/components/ping.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/components/ping.py) starts a server with the options, connects one client
and leaves it idle for half a second:

```bash
pip install websockets
python examples/components/ping.py
```

```text
response: observation
the server measured the connection's RTT from its pings: 0.17 ms
```

The second line is a side benefit: each pong tells the server the connection's round-trip time (RTT), which `websockets`
keeps as `connection.latency`.

## Why 100 ms

The robot's silence must stay shorter than its retransmission timeout, which is about its RTT plus 200 ms.
A WebSocket server sends its next ping one interval after the last pong came back, so the robot is silent for the
interval plus one RTT. An interval under 200 ms is therefore sufficient on a link of any length, and at 100 ms a
ping that is lost still leaves the next one inside the limit.

Measured on an RTT of 11.7 ms: pings 190 ms apart still kept the window (an upload after a pause took 1.18
round trips), and pings 250 ms apart did not (2.04). Anything from 25 to 190 ms apart measured the same.

## What was measured

| Link | Upload | Without the ping | With it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Machines of one cloud provider, RTTs of 11.7 and 69.2 ms, 20 samples per cell | 100 KB after 500 ms of silence | 3.0 round trips | 1.1 |
| the same | 500 KB | 3.0 | 1.1 |
| the same | 1 MB | 3.0 | 1.25 |
| Two cloud machines, RTTs of 11, 21, 41 and 81 ms, 40 uploads per cell, over a WebSocket whose server has `ping.websockets_options()` | 100 KB, 0.53 s after each response | 3.3, 2.1, 2.0 and 2.0 round trips | 1.2, 1.1, 1.0 and 1.0 |

A window that the pings do not fill still shrinks. BBR on the robot keeps that one: `window.keep(sock)`, or
`connect()`. With 1% loss, BBR kept the window: none of 40 uploads took an extra round trip
([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#with-1-packet-loss)).

## When the server cannot ping

**A plain HTTP server.** A server that answers one HTTP request with one response has no way to send anything
unsolicited. There the ping comes from the robot. `connect()` does it by itself:

```python
from sequence_ai.network import connect

link_user = connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")     # a small GET after each 100 ms of idle time
```

**A WebSocket server you cannot change.** Ping from the client side, on the connection your client already holds.
With openpi's client it is one line, `openpi.keep(policy)`: see
[How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md) With your own `websockets`
client:

```python
from websockets.sync.client import connect as ws_connect
from sequence_ai.network import window

with ws_connect("ws://YOUR_GPU:8000") as ws_user:
    window.keep(ws_user.socket)                               # BBR on its socket, where the machine allows

    def ping_user() -> None:
        if not ws_user.ping().wait(5.0):                      # no pong in 5 s: the connection is gone
            raise TimeoutError("no pong")

    warm_user = window.Warm(ping_user)                        # a ping after each 100 ms of idle time
    ws_user.send(observation_user)
    response_user = ws_user.recv()
    warm_user.used()                                          # after each request and response
```

Run against a stand-in server on one machine, that client sent four pings in 0.45 seconds of idle time.

## Tested

- `tests/network/test_ping.py` starts a `websockets` server with the options and checks that it pings every interval and
  that one without them does not. It does the same under uvicorn.
- uvicorn 0.54 takes the options on its `auto`, `websockets-sansio` and `websockets` implementations. uvicorn 0.39's
  `websockets-sansio` sends no pings, so on an older uvicorn leave `ws` at `auto` or pass `ws="websockets"`.
- The first three rows of the table were taken with the tool in [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench), whose server pings on
  request, and not with a policy server.
- The WebSocket row was taken with [`bench/ws_bench.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/ws_bench.py): a `websockets` server with the
  options, and no policy behind it. [What do the components save?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md) has every cell.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md

# How do I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its outputs?

Replay the module your policy calls many times per run, its denoiser, from CUDA graphs captured from its own eager
kernels. `cuda_graphs.install` does that in one call, and keeps a graph only when its output equals eager mode's byte
for byte. On GR00T N1.7 on an L4 this reduced a run from 224 ms to 146 ms (1.54 times faster) with exactly the same
actions. It gains nothing on a model that already fuses and graphs its kernels.

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import cuda_graphs

cuda_graphs.install(model_user, ["action_head.denoiser"])    # model.action_head.denoiser, graphed in place
model_user(observation_user)                                       # a new shape: run in eager mode, captured, checked
model_user(observation_user)                                       # replayed
```

Nothing else in your code changes. The module stays where it is in your model, the same object of the same class,
with its weights, its `state_dict` and its hooks unchanged. Only its `forward` is replaced.

## Why this is faster

A vision-language-action policy with a diffusion or flow action head calls its denoiser several times per inference.
In eager PyTorch at batch 1, each of those calls launches many small kernels one by one, and launch overhead
dominates: on GR00T N1.7 on an L4 the GPU was busy 41% of the time. A CUDA graph replays the same kernels as one
launch.

## Why the outputs do not change

A graph replays the same kernels that eager mode ran, in the same order, so its arithmetic is identical. A compiler
that fuses kernels changes the order of the arithmetic, and with it the outputs. The three were measured on the same
model and GPU:

| Approach | Speed | Outputs |
|---|---|---|
| `torch.compile(backend="cudagraphs")` | 1.00× (225 ms) | unchanged |
| `torch.compile`, inductor | 1.45× | changed: 0.0051 apart on average |
| `cuda_graphs` | 1.54× (224 ms to 146 ms) | exactly the same, on inputs it was not captured on |

GR00T N1.7, one L4, its DiT captured. One model and one GPU: **these are not numbers for your model.**

`cuda_graphs` verifies the equality instead of assuming it. Each new shape is run in eager mode once, captured, and
replayed on the same inputs; the graph is kept only if the two outputs are equal byte for byte. A shape whose capture
fails or differs runs in eager mode from then on, which is reported once.

## Which module to name

One that is called more than once per run with the same shapes. To find it, count the calls over a few runs:

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import cuda_graphs

census_user = cuda_graphs.Census(cuda_graphs.modules_of(model_user))
for _ in range(3):
    model_user(observation_user)                                   # one inference, as your code makes it
    census_user.end_act()
census_user.close()
paths_user = [row_user["path"] for row_user in census_user.candidates()]    # the outermost and slowest first
cuda_graphs.install(model_user, paths_user[:1])
```

[`examples/graph_a_module.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/graph_a_module.py) does all of it on a small flow-style model, and runs on
a machine with no GPU, where it prints which module it would graph and leaves the model unchanged.

## Check it on your GPU

```python
import torch
from sequence_ai.engine import cuda_graphs

torch.manual_seed(0)                                     # a policy that draws noise: the same noise for each run
eager_user = model_user(observation_user)
cuda_graphs.install(model_user, paths_user[:1])
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_user(observation_user)  # a new shape: captured, and checked against eager mode here
torch.manual_seed(0)
print(cuda_graphs.same(eager_user, model_user(observation_user)))       # True: a replayed run, byte for byte
cuda_graphs.ACTIVE = False                               # the same model in eager mode again, to compare timings
```

[`examples/check_on_a_gpu.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/check_on_a_gpu.py) runs the capture on a real GPU and compares every
output with eager mode's. On a T4, its small flow-style model went from 16.1 ms to 2.4 ms per run: byte for byte on
inputs the capture never saw, the model's random noise unchanged, a new batch size captured automatically.

## What it is safe against

- **A graph whose output differs is never used.**
- **A failed capture does not change your model's random noise.** The GPU's random generator is swapped for a clone
  while a capture runs, and restored afterwards.
- **What your model checks about its module still holds:** `isinstance`, its type, its methods and its hooks, which
  fire around a replayed call too.

## When it applies

- **A PyTorch model that launches many small kernels.** A model that already fuses and compiles its kernels, such as
  π0.5 under JAX at 98% GPU-busy, has no launch overhead to remove.
- **A module called many times per run.** A module called once has one launch sequence to save.
- **Shapes that repeat.** Each new shape is captured and checked once, so a module gains from a shape's second call
  on. A prompt of a new length is a new shape, captured the first time it occurs.
- **A CUDA GPU.** Without one, nothing is graphed, which is reported once, and the model runs as before.
- **torch 2.4 or later,** which lets a capture swap the GPU's random generator; with an earlier torch, nothing is
  captured.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md

# How do I measure the link between my robot and my GPU?

Run one file where the GPU is and one where the robot is. The client prints how many round trips an upload takes after a
pause, with a ping through the pause, back to back, and as a camera stream. That tells you which network components
help on your link and which do not.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai && cd sequence-ai     # on both machines
python3 bench/server.py --port 9000                        # where the GPU is
python3 bench/client.py --host GPU_ADDRESS --port 9000     # where the robot is
```

Both files are standard library only and run on Linux and macOS. Nothing needs installing, and no model is involved.
With the defaults a run takes about 100 seconds plus the time the uploads take on your link.

## What it prints

This is a run of the defaults with both ends on one machine. Loopback involves no network, so these numbers indicate
nothing about any link. They are here to show the table's format.

```text
host 127.0.0.1  handshake 0.2 ms  baseline rtt min 0.1 / p50 0.2 ms  congestion None
mode            size    p50 ms    p95 ms    p99 ms   x rtt
idle          100000       0.3       0.5         -    1.54
ping          100000       0.2       0.3         -    1.04
continuous    100000       0.0       0.1         -    0.20
idle          500000       0.2       0.4         -    1.14
ping          500000       0.3       0.4         -    1.29
continuous    500000       0.1       0.1         -    0.55
idle         1000000       0.4       0.7         -    2.09
ping         1000000       0.3       0.6         -    1.69
continuous   1000000       0.2       0.3         -    1.14
30Hz           50000       0.2       0.3       0.3    1.00
10Hz          100000       0.2       0.3       0.3    1.19
10Hz          500000       0.3       0.5       0.6    1.29
```

- **The first line** is the link itself: how long the TCP handshake took, the round-trip time (RTT) with no data on it
  (`baseline`), and the congestion control the connection uses (`None` where the system does not report it, as on
  macOS).
- **`mode`** is what was sent, and **`size`** how many bytes each upload had.
- **`p50`, `p95`, `p99`** are how long an upload took to be acknowledged. `p99` is given for streams only, which have
  enough frames for it.
- **`x rtt`** is the median over the baseline RTT: how many round trips an upload took. This is the column to
  read.

It also writes `result.json` with every sample and the kernel's state of the connection around each upload.

## What each block sends

| Block | What it sends | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| `baseline` | an empty frame and its ack | the RTT with no data on it |
| `idle` | a frame, then a pause, then the next | what a pause between uploads costs |
| `ping` | as `idle`, the server pinging through the pause | whether a ping from the server side keeps the window |
| `keepwarm` | as `idle`, the robot sending a byte through the pause | the same, done from the client side |
| `continuous` | the next frame as soon as the last is acknowledged | the upload with a warm window |
| `stream` | frames at a fixed rate, acks not waited for | what each frame of a camera stream costs |
| `twowrite` | a frame in two writes with Nagle on | what a header and a body written apart cost |

The defaults run `idle`, `ping`, `continuous` and `stream`, with uploads of 100 KB, 500 KB and 1 MB, 500 ms of
silence, a ping every 100 ms, and 20 samples of each.

## How to read your result

| You see | It means | What to add |
|---|---|---|
| `idle` near 2 or 3, `continuous` near 1 | A pause costs your uploads extra round trips | A ping or BBR: the next two rows show which |
| `ping` or `keepwarm` near 1 | A ping through the pause keeps the window | `connect()` on the robot, or [`ping`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-keep-a-websocket-policy-servers-connection-warm.md) on a WebSocket server |
| `ping` no better than `idle` | A ping does not help on this link | Run again with `--bbr`; if that is near 1, use `window` |
| `idle` and `continuous` both near 1 | The pause costs nothing here | Nothing for the pause |
| `stream` rows well above 1 | Frames wait on the link: loss, or the last hop | Look at the last hop first: `wifi_power.check()` on the robot |
| A large `baseline` | The GPU is far away | [A GPU nearer the robot](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md) |

## Match the run to your robot

The defaults measure large uploads after half a second of silence. To measure what your robot sends, give its sizes
and its pace:

```bash
# a robot that acts every 0.53 s with 24 KB of frames: the pause, a ping from each side, then BBR
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle,ping,keepwarm --warm 1m
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle --warm 1m --bbr
```

| Flag | What it sets | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--sizes` | frame sizes for `idle`, `ping`, `keepwarm` and `continuous` | `100k,500k,1m` |
| `--idle-ms` | the silence after each ack | `500` |
| `--ping-ms` | the interval of the pings and of the robot's bytes | `100` |
| `--stream` | camera streams, as `HZxSIZE` | `30x50k,10x100k,10x500k` |
| `--seconds` | how long each stream runs | `10` |
| `--samples` | samples for each block and size | `20` |
| `--modes` | the blocks to run, in order | `idle,ping,continuous,stream` |
| `--bbr` | request BBR on this connection's socket | off |
| `--warm` | upload one frame of this size before measuring | none |
| `--out` | where the samples are written | `result.json` |

## Try other distances from one pair of machines

On Linux, as root, where the client sends from:

```bash
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 80ms          # about 80 ms more on the round trip
sudo tc qdisc change dev eth0 root netem delay 80ms loss 1%
sudo tc qdisc del dev eth0 root
```

## Reference measurements

| Link | Upload | After 500 ms of silence | Server pinging every 100 ms | One after another |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Three machines of one cloud provider, RTTs of 11.7 and 69.2 ms, 20 samples per cell | 100 KB | 3.0 round trips | 1.1 | 1.05 |
| the same | 500 KB | 3.0 | 1.1 | 1.1 |
| the same | 1 MB | 3.0 | 1.25 | 1.3 |

[`bench/README.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/README.md) has these in full, and
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
table for a robot that sends two requests per second.

## Measure a server that is already running

The tool above measures the link with its own server. To see the link while your policy server runs, read it off the
server's kernel (Linux):

```python
from sequence_ai.network import tcp_link

tcp_link.read(sock_user)             # any connected socket: rtt_ms, rttvar_ms, retrans, total_retrans, cwnd
tcp_link.of(scope_user["client"])    # in an ASGI app served with one_write_http(): this request's own connection
```

and on the robot, `link.stats()["latency_us"]["act_us"]` gives each request's p50, p95 and p99 as the robot saw them.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md

# How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?

Start with the link, because LeRobot 0.7's remote inference already manages the robot's timing itself: put the
policy server near the robot, measure the link, and keep the link from going idle between observations. `sequence-ai`
has one small component for the last of these, a Zenoh setting, and it is the only thing here that touches LeRobot.

```python
from sequence_ai.network import lerobot

path_user = lerobot.keep_alive_file("zenoh-keep-alive.json5")     # an idle link then sends a frame every 100 ms
```

```bash
pip install sequence-ai          # it needs neither LeRobot nor Zenoh to write the file
```

Give the file to both sides, since each side sends its own frames:

| Side | LeRobot's setting | As a flag |
|---|---|---|
| The GPU: `lerobot-policy-server` | `zenoh.config_file` | `--zenoh.config_file=zenoh-keep-alive.json5` |
| The robot: `lerobot-rollout --inference.type=remote` | `zenoh_config_path` | `--inference.zenoh_config_path=zenoh-keep-alive.json5` |

The setting names are read from LeRobot 0.7.0's source (`ZenohConfig.config_file` in `transport/zenoh.py`,
`RemoteInferenceConfig.zenoh_config_path` in `inference/factory.py`). The flags follow from them the way LeRobot's
other flags do.

## Tested

- **Verified:** Zenoh 1.10.2 takes the setting. With the file, an idle link between two Zenoh peers on one machine sent
  a frame about every 100 ms each way; without it, a frame every 1.5 s or less often. `tests/network/test_lerobot.py`
  repeats this when Zenoh is installed.
- **From source inspection:** LeRobot loads `config_file` first and then sets only its own keys over it (the
  mode, the endpoints, discovery, shared memory and the connect timeout), so a transport setting written in the file
  stays.
- **Measured on a real link:** two Zenoh peers on two cloud machines, one answering the
  other's requests. A 100 KB request 0.53 s after each response took 38.1, 44.8, 82.8 and 164.3 ms at round-trip times
  (RTTs) of 11, 21, 41 and 81 ms, and 13.9, 23.2, 42.3 and 82.2 ms with the file on both ends: two to three round trips
  became one, on 40 of 40 requests. [What do the network components save?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md) has the table.

## Try it

[`examples/quickstart_lerobot.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_lerobot.py) writes the file and prints where to set it on each
side:

```bash
python examples/quickstart_lerobot.py
```

```text
wrote zenoh-keep-alive.json5:
{
  "transport": {
    "link": {
      "tx": {
        "keep_alive": 100
      }
    }
  }
}
on the GPU, the policy server's setting:   zenoh.config_file = zenoh-keep-alive.json5
on the robot, remote inference's setting:  zenoh_config_path = zenoh-keep-alive.json5
```

`keep_alive` is how many keep-alive frames a Zenoh link sends in one lease. The lease is 10 seconds unless you
changed it, so 100 frames per lease is one every 100 ms. The lease itself is unchanged: it is how long a silent peer
is waited for, and a short one drops a robot whose Wi-Fi stalls for a moment.

**You already have a Zenoh file**, for TLS or access control. LeRobot takes one file, so put both in it:

```python
mine_user = {"transport": {"link": {"tls": {"root_ca_certificate": "ca.pem"}}}}
path_user = lerobot.keep_alive_file("zenoh.json5", base=mine_user)     # your settings, with the keep-alive beside them
```

Zenoh 1.10.2 loaded that file with both settings in it.

## Why an idle link costs anything

On Linux, a TCP connection that has sent nothing for longer than its retransmission timeout, which is at least its
RTT plus 200 ms, has its congestion window restarted. The next observation can then take more round trips to upload
than it would on a warm connection. A link that sends a small frame every 100 ms is never idle that long.
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
measurements, including the links where the pause cost nothing.

## The other things that set the latency

**The distance.** The RTT between robot and GPU is incurred on every request, whatever else is done.
[Measure it](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md), and if the GPU is far,
[get one nearer](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md).

**LeRobot's own settings.** These are LeRobot's, from the `RemoteInferenceConfig` of 0.7.0:

| Setting | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `encoding` | `"raw"` | `"jpeg"` sends camera frames as JPEG, at `jpeg_quality` (90), which makes each upload smaller |
| `refill_seconds` | `0.5` | Request the next chunk when this much playback is left; never less than the recent longest turnaround plus one action interval |
| `chunk_merge` | `"auto"` | How a new chunk is merged with the one being executed: `"append"` or `"aligned"` |
| `max_observation_age_s` | `5.0` | The oldest observation that is still acted on |

**The robot's machine.**

- `window.keep()` sets BBR on one socket. It cannot reach LeRobot's sockets, because Zenoh opens its own.
  The machine-wide settings do reach them, and both need root:
  `sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr` (after `sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`), or
  `sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0`.
- On Wi-Fi, check power saving. This reads the machine's settings and changes nothing:

  ```python
  from sequence_ai.network import wifi_power

  wifi_power.check()    # the interface whose power saving is on, having warned how to turn it off; else None
  ```

## What this package does not add to LeRobot

LeRobot's remote inference has its own transport, message format and client, so `connect()`, `msgpack_io`,
`compress` and `one_write` do not apply to it. LeRobot already requests the next chunk ahead of time based on
the turnaround it measured, aligns a new chunk with the one being executed, and can send frames as JPEG.
[The comparison page](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/comparison.md) describes what each does, from source.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md

# How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?

Run openpi's own policy server on the GPU and openpi's own client on the robot, as openpi's guide describes.
`sequence-ai` then changes the command that starts the server, and two lines on the robot: the server pings each robot
and takes its pictures as JPEG, and the robot sends them that way and keeps its connection from going idle between
action chunks.

On the GPU, in openpi's repository. openpi's `docs/remote_inference.md` starts the server with
`uv run scripts/serve_policy.py --env=DROID`, on port 8000; this runs the same script, unchanged:

```bash
uv run --with sequence-ai python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi scripts/serve_policy.py --env=DROID
```

On the robot:

```python
from openpi_client import websocket_client_policy
from sequence_ai.network import openpi
from sequence_ai.network.openpi import image_tools      # was: from openpi_client import image_tools

policy_user = websocket_client_policy.WebsocketClientPolicy(host="YOUR_GPU", port=8000)
# keeps the connection warm
kept_user = openpi.keep(policy_user)
observation_user["observation/exterior_image_1_left"] = image_tools.resize_with_pad(frame_user, 224, 224)  # now a JPEG
# openpi's own call, unchanged
action_chunk_user = policy_user.infer(observation_user)["actions"]
```

```bash
pip install sequence-ai          # on the robot: no extra needed. The GPU's command above brings its own.
```

π0 and π0.5 are the models; openpi is the repository that serves them. Nothing of openpi's is replaced here: the
client, the server, the msgpack layout and the responses stay openpi's own. A server started this way serves a robot
that sends arrays as before, and `keep()` needs nothing of the server; a robot that sends its pictures as JPEG needs the
server started this way.

## What the lines do

| Line | What it does | When it applies |
|---|---|---|
| `python -m sequence_ai.network.openpi`, on the GPU | openpi's server pings each connection every 100 ms, and hands its policy each picture sent as JPEG as the array it reads | always; a picture sent as an array reaches the policy as before |
| `image_tools` from `sequence_ai.network.openpi`, on the robot | `resize_with_pad` fits each picture exactly as openpi's does, then returns it as base64 JPEG at quality 95; `convert_to_uint8` returns that as it is | always; the server must be started as above |
| `openpi.keep(policy)`, on the robot | BBR as the socket's congestion control | Linux, with the kernel's BBR module loaded (`sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`) |
| | TCP keepalive | every machine that takes the options |
| | A WebSocket ping each 100 ms the connection is idle, for 60 s after the last `infer()` | always |

A robot that executes an action chunk before requesting the next one leaves its connection silent in between. On
Linux, a connection silent for longer than its retransmission timeout has its congestion window restarted, so the
next observation can take more round trips to upload.
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
mechanism and the links where it did and did not cost anything. The pings keep the connection from going silent while
the server can answer them; openpi's server answers none while it runs inference, so on a Linux robot without BBR the
window can still be halved once before each upload ([measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)). BBR on the robot avoids that.
JPEG makes the upload itself smaller: two 224 x 224 pictures are 301,056 bytes as arrays.

`kept.bbr` reports whether the socket accepted BBR, `kept.congestion` which congestion control it now uses, and
`kept.warm.pings` how many pings were answered. `kept.close()` stops the pings; the connection stays openpi's.

In a server script of your own, call `openpi.patch()` before it makes openpi's `WebsocketPolicyServer`: that is what the
command does before it runs `scripts/serve_policy.py`. `patch()` needs openpi's own `websocket_policy_server.py`; any
other server is refused with `TypeError`.

## Try it without a GPU or a checkpoint

[`examples/quickstart_openpi.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_openpi.py) starts a stand-in server on your machine that
speaks openpi's protocol, then runs openpi's real client against it with the one line added. It needs openpi's client
(`packages/openpi-client` in openpi's repository, `pip install -e .`).

```bash
python examples/quickstart_openpi.py
```

Run in a new environment with sequence-ai 0.62.0 and openpi-client 0.1.2, on a Mac, it printed:

```text
BBR on its socket: False; TCP keepalive options accepted: 4
infer 0: a chunk of 10 actions
infer 1: a chunk of 10 actions
infer 2: a chunk of 10 actions
pings answered while it was idle: 12
```

Twelve pings is four in each of the three half-second pauses. BBR is `False` because a Mac has none.

Against a real openpi server, [`examples/openpi_robot.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/openpi_robot.py) takes its host and port.

## Or serve the policy with `serve()`

To serve several robots in batches, or to give the robot `connect()` in place of openpi's client, serve the policy with
`sequence_ai.serve()` in openpi's environment on the GPU:

```python
from openpi.policies import policy_config
from openpi.training import config as openpi_config

import sequence_ai
from sequence_ai.engine import openpi

policy_user = policy_config.create_trained_policy(openpi_config.get_config("pi05_droid"), checkpoint_dir_user)
sequence_ai.serve(openpi.batched(policy_user), batch=[1, 2, 4, 8], example=observation_user)  # or serve(policy.infer)
```

On the robot, the observation keeps openpi's keys, and `act()` returns what openpi's `infer()` returns:

```python
import sequence_ai

link_user = sequence_ai.connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")
# observation["observation/exterior_image_1_left"]: the frame
action_chunk_user = link_user.act(observation_user)["actions"]
```

`openpi.batched(policy)` passes each observation through the policy's transforms, as `infer()` does, and samples all of
them in one call, each with its own noise. The policy's JAX model compiles each listed batch size once, in the warm-up
on `example`. A PyTorch checkpoint runs its observations one by one. Every default of [What is on by
default](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/what-is-on-by-default.md) applies: the robot sends each 224×224 picture as JPEG, the server turns it back into
the array the policy reads. At quality 95, JPEG moved π0.5's actions by 5.9% on average, a tenth of the policy's own
run-to-run noise; `jpeg=False` sends exact pixels.

## Tested

- **Verified:** `openpi.keep()` against openpi-client 0.1.2 on a local connection, as above and in
  `tests/network/test_openpi.py`.
- **Verified:** `openpi.batched()` against stand-ins of openpi's model and transforms: one call to the model per
  batch, each observation's own transforms and output (`tests/engine/test_openpi.py`).
- **Verified:** the server's pings and its decoding, and `image_tools`, against a server module built as openpi's
  `websocket_policy_server.py` is, on a local connection; and the command, against a script run as
  `scripts/serve_policy.py` is (`tests/network/test_openpi_server.py`).
- **Measured on a real link:** `keep()` on a WebSocket connection of the kind openpi's client
  holds (the `websockets` library on both ends, compression off, a stand-in for the client class), between two cloud
  machines. A 100 KB upload 0.53 s after each response took 37.6, 44.4, 82.4 and 163.8 ms at round-trip times (RTTs) of
  11, 21, 41 and 81 ms, and 12.7, 22.7, 41.8 and 82.6 ms with `keep()`: two to three round trips became one, on 40 of 40
  uploads. [What do the network components save?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md) has the table.
- **Measured with openpi's own server and client:** one closed-loop run with π0.5 (`pi05_droid`) on an L4, the client in
  a Linux virtual machine on a home connection, 301 KB per request. The time a request spent outside inference had a
  median of 181 and 152 ms in two episodes without `keep()`; with it, 92 ms in an episode without packet loss and 157 ms
  in one that lost packets; with the BBR module loaded as well, 86 and 91 ms.
  [The table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#openpikeep-with-openpis-own-server-and-client) has the idle times and the congestion
  window.
- **Measured with openpi's own server and client, the pictures as JPEG:** one closed-loop run with π0.5 on an L4, the
  robot a simulated arm on a Mac on a home connection, the server pinging. Each request's upload went from 301.5 KB to
  18.8 KB, and the time it spent outside the server, beyond one RTT, from about 97 to about 21 ms at the median.
  [The table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#pictures-as-jpeg-with-openpis-own-server-and-client).

## What openpi already does

openpi's client and server already do several things a remote policy needs, so this package has no component for them:

- **One connection, kept open.** The client connects once and reuses the WebSocket for every `infer()`.
- **Arrays as raw bytes.** Observations and responses are sent as msgpack with numpy arrays as raw bytes.
- **Images resized on the robot.** openpi's guide resizes each image on the client with
  `image_tools.resize_with_pad(img, 224, 224)` before sending it, as an array.
- **Action chunks executed open-loop.** `ActionChunkBroker` requests a new chunk only when the current one is
  exhausted.

If you write your own server or client for an openpi model, `msgpack_io` reads openpi's array layout,
`frames.resize_image(..., mode="pad", filter="bilinear")` is openpi's `resize_with_pad`, byte for byte, and
`frames.decode` turns a picture sent as JPEG back into its array. [The comparison page](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/comparison.md) sets the two
side by side.

## If something fails

- `TypeError: this client keeps no WebSocket connection at _ws`: pass the `WebsocketClientPolicy` itself to
  `keep()`, not an `ActionChunkBroker` wrapped around it. Keep the broker for `infer()`.
- `RuntimeError: Error in inference server:` on the robot, after its pictures went as JPEG: the server was started
  without `sequence_ai.network.openpi`, so its policy was handed the pictures as text. Start it with the command above,
  or import `image_tools` from `openpi_client` again.
- `ValueError: observation/...: not a JPEG or PNG image` in the server's traceback: a picture under that key came as
  text or bytes that are not one. Send it as `image_tools` makes it, or as an array.
- `TypeError: this server is not built as openpi's websocket_policy_server.py is`: the openpi on the GPU starts its
  server another way than `patch()` was written for. Start it with openpi's own command, and send arrays.
- `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'typing_extensions'` on importing `openpi_client`: openpi-client 0.1.0 imports
  it without listing it as a dependency, so a new environment may lack it. `pip install typing_extensions`.
- The client prints nothing and never returns: while the connection is refused it retries every 5 seconds, so the
  server is not up yet or the port is wrong. This is read from openpi's source, not made to happen here.

More in the [FAQ](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/faq.md#with-openpi-and-lerobot).

## Where the GPU comes from

Any GPU the robot can reach on port 8000. [How do I get a GPU near my robot?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md)
covers the case where you have none nearby. The robot's code changes in one place: the `host`.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-send-each-act-over-two-uplinks.md

# How do I send each act over two uplinks?

A robot with two ways out - a Starlink terminal and a cellular modem, say - can send each act over both and use
whichever answer comes back first. A slow moment on one line then costs nothing while the other is quick, and a line
that drops leaves the acts to the other.

```python
import sequence_ai

robot_user = sequence_ai.connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000", lines=["eth0", "wwan0"])   # one connection by each interface
robot_user.wait_until_ready()
action_user = robot_user.act(observation_user)               # sent on both lines; the first answer
print(robot_user.stats()["lines"])                           # each line's acts, first answers and errors
```

`lines=` names two or more of the robot's network interfaces, one uplink each, for a policy server at an address: one
started with `serve()` on your own GPU, or on a GPU you rent. `ip link` lists a Linux machine's interfaces, and
`ifconfig` a Mac's; a name the machine does not have is refused with the names it has.

## What it does

- **Each act goes on every line at once.** The observation is packed once, and the same body goes on each line's own
  connection, bound to its interface before it connects, so it leaves by that line whatever the default route.
- **The first answer is used.** The others are read when they come. An act fails only when every line has failed.
- **The policy runs once.** The copies of an act carry one request id, `X-Seq-Request-Id`; `serve()` runs the policy
  once for them and gives each copy that answer, and says so with `once` in its `X-Seq-Reads` header. To a server
  that does not say `once`, each act goes on one line alone, the first that is free, and on the next only when that
  one could not connect: an act is never run twice.
- **A line that stops answering collects no queue.** A line still carrying the act before is not given the next one.
- **Each line stays warm.** Each line's connection keeps its own pings when idle, as one connection does
  ([What is on by default](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/what-is-on-by-default.md)).

Where the server has another address by each line - IPv6 on one, IPv4 alone on the other - name each line's:

```python
robot_user = sequence_ai.connect(url_user, lines={"eth0": "http://[2001:db8::7]:8000",     # IPv6 by the terminal
                                                  "wwan0": "http://203.0.113.7:8000"})     # IPv4 by the modem
```

With an address by each line, each act first compares the servers the lines' pings named: where their process, version
or start time differ, the lines reach two servers, and the act raises `ValueError` and is sent on none.

## On a GPU rented from General Sequences

With a follow token, each line's address is let into the GPU's allow list before the robot connects, each by a follow
that goes out by that line:

```python
robot_user = sequence_ai.connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000", follow=follow_token_user, lines=["eth0", "wwan0"])
```

`seq gpu follow --line wwan0` does the same for one line from a shell, and `seq gpu list` says where each line was let
in from. [How do I get a GPU near my robot?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md) has the follow token.

A line follows over the address family it reaches the GPU by. Over IPv4, a cellular or satellite line's public address
is usually shared by many of its provider's customers (carrier-grade NAT), and letting that address in lets them all in.
Where `seq gpu list` shows the GPU an IPv6 address, connect to that address or to the GPU's name, so that each line
with IPv6 follows over it; and start the server with a token either way (`serve(policy, token=...)`).

## What it costs

Every act's body is sent on each line: two lines, twice the upload. Two cameras' pictures as JPEG are about 24 KB an
act ([`frames.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/frames.py) has the measurement), so a policy asked every 533 ms, as π0.5 is,
sends about 160 MB an hour on each line. On a line billed by the gigabyte, count it. The answers come back on each line
too, but an answer is a chunk of actions, small beside the pictures.

## Check both lines

```bash
python -m sequence_ai.check http://YOUR_GPU:8000 --lines eth0,wwan0
```

Beside its other lines, it pings the server by each interface and says whether the server runs an act's copies once.
With an observation (the server's example, or `--observation FILE`), it sends 5 acts on every line and says how many
each line answered first, and how many megabytes an hour each line sends at one act a second.

## Needs

Linux 5.7 or later, or macOS: no root, since either lets a program bind its own socket to an interface. A policy
reached by its deployment's name is reached over one line.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md

# How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?

Give your model to `sequence_ai.serve()` as a function, and call it from the robot with `connect()`. Everything here is
open source and runs on a GPU you already have: no account and no service of ours is involved.

On the GPU:

```python
import sequence_ai

def policy_user(observation_user):                    # your model: one observation in, what the robot needs out
    return {"actions": model_user(observation_user["image"], observation_user["state"])}

sequence_ai.serve(policy_user, port=8000, example=observation_user)
```

On the robot:

```python
import sequence_ai

link_user = sequence_ai.connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")
actions_user = link_user.act({"image": frame_user, "state": state_user})["actions"]
```

Both sides' defaults are on: the robot sends pictures as JPEG and compresses large arrays where that saves time, keeps
its one connection warm with pings, and waits longer for the first answer; the server runs the policy on a thread of
its own, answers pings at once, warms the policy up on `example`, and sends torch and JAX outputs back as numpy arrays.
[What is on by default, and how do I turn each part off?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/what-is-on-by-default.md) lists every part with its switch,
and `python -m sequence_ai.check http://YOUR_GPU:8000` says which are on between your robot and your server.

[`quickstart_server.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_server.py) is this server in one short file, with a stand-in
`policy_user` to replace. The [Quickstart](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md) runs both sides on one machine first, with the output of each
step. Run between two addresses of one machine, the robot printed:

```text
request 0: 8 actions of 7 numbers, the first [128. 128. 128.]
request 1: 8 actions of 7 numbers, the first [128. 128. 128.]
request 2: 8 actions of 7 numbers, the first [128. 128. 128.]
3 requests, the slowest took 3.4 ms
```

## Your model, as a function

`serve()` takes any model as a function. It is called with the observation the robot sent, a dict with numpy arrays as
arrays, and returns what the robot gets back: a dict, an array or a list, with numpy arrays, torch tensors or JAX
arrays in it.

Return an action chunk: the steps the robot plays while it asks for the next one. A policy that returns one step at a
time, a network round trip away, leaves a 30 Hz arm waiting for each step: OpenVLA, which returns one step, held a
simulated arm still for all 1,200 steps of a 40 s run.

| Your model | What to pass |
|---|---|
| A function of one observation | `serve(policy)` |
| A function of a list of observations, one forward pass for all of them | `serve(policy_on_a_list, batch=[1, 2, 4, 8])` |
| openpi (π0, π0.5) | `serve(policy.infer)`, or batched: `serve(openpi.batched(policy), batch=[1, 2, 4, 8])` |
| A PyTorch module: LeRobot's, GR00T's, your own | a function that turns the observation into the module's inputs and calls it |

A PyTorch module, as [`serve_a_pytorch_model.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/serve_a_pytorch_model.py) serves one:

```python
import torch

@torch.inference_mode()
def policy_user(observation_user):
    # 1x3xHxW
    image_user = torch.as_tensor(observation_user["image"], device="cuda").permute(2, 0, 1)[None].float() / 255
    state_user = torch.as_tensor(observation_user["state"], device="cuda")[None]
    return {"actions": model_user(image_user, state_user)[0]}            # a tensor: serve() sends it as a numpy array

sequence_ai.serve(policy_user, example=observation_user)
```

Run on a CPU, its robot printed:

```text
a ndarray of shape (8, 7) and dtype float32 from the model on the cpu: the first [ 0.0413 -0.3051  0.1673]
```

An openpi policy, batched:

```python
from openpi.policies import policy_config
from openpi.training import config as openpi_config

import sequence_ai
from sequence_ai.engine import openpi

policy_user = policy_config.create_trained_policy(openpi_config.get_config("pi05_droid"), checkpoint_dir_user)
sequence_ai.serve(openpi.batched(policy_user), batch=[1, 2, 4, 8], example=observation_user)
```

`openpi.batched(policy)` is openpi's own `infer()` for a list of observations: each passes through the policy's
transforms, and the model samples all of them in one call. [`openpi.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/openpi.py) has the
details.

**Batching.** With `batch=[1, 2, 4, 8]`, the observations that wait while the policy runs reach it together, in the
largest listed size they fill, and each robot gets its own output back. Five robots acting at the same moment against
[`components/serve.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/components/serve.py) printed:

```text
5 robots, each with its own actions: the first of each [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
the warm-up ran batches of [1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8]; the robots' acts reached the model as batches of [4, 1]
```

The batches depend on when the requests arrive: on another run the same five came as `[2, 2, 1]`. List the sizes your
model is compiled or graphed for: a batch of an unlisted size is never sent to it. Batching serves several robots in
fewer forward passes; one robot's request is no faster for it.

## You already have a server

Keep it. `connect()` needs two things from a server: a POST that takes a msgpack body and responds with msgpack or
JSON, and any cheap GET for its ping. To get the rest of the defaults, a server also says what it restores in an
`X-Seq-Reads` header and restores it, and says it is a sequence-ai server in `X-Seq-Server`. In a FastAPI app:

```python
import asyncio

import numpy as np
import uvicorn
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response

from sequence_ai.network import compressed, frames, msgpack_io
from sequence_ai.network.one_write import WholeResponse, one_write_http

app_user = FastAPI()
# so the robot sends JPEG, compressed
SAYS_user = {"X-Seq-Reads": "jpeg, zstd, zlib", "X-Seq-Server": "sequence-ai/0.63.0"}


def policy_user(observation_user: dict) -> np.ndarray:
    return np.full((8, 7), float(observation_user["image"].mean()), dtype=np.float32)      # your model here


@app_user.post("/act")
async def act_user(request_user: Request) -> Response:
    observation_user, _ = compressed.expand(msgpack_io.unpack(await request_user.body()), limit=64 << 20)
    observation_user = frames.unpack_pictures(observation_user)               # each picture sent as JPEG, as its array
    actions_user = await asyncio.to_thread(policy_user, observation_user)          # the model runs off the event loop
    return Response(msgpack_io.pack({"actions": actions_user}), media_type=msgpack_io.MEDIA_TYPE, headers=SAYS_user)


@app_user.get("/ping")
async def ping_user() -> Response:
    return Response(headers=SAYS_user)                                   # all the robot's ping needs: an empty response


if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run(WholeResponse(app_user), host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, http=one_write_http())
```

This file was run with FastAPI 0.163 against the quickstart's robot: three requests answered, the second and third with
their picture sent as JPEG (the first left before the robot had heard what the server reads; `link.wait_until_ready()`
hears it first). `asyncio.to_thread` runs the model on a pool of threads, so two robots' requests can run it at once;
`serve()` runs it on one thread, one call at a time.

Your paths can have other names: `connect(url, act_path="/infer", ping_path="/healthz")`.

## You already have a client

Keep that too, and take single components. Each is one file and imports no other component:

```python
import httpx
from sequence_ai.network import window

transport_user = httpx.HTTPTransport(socket_options=window.socket_options())    # BBR and TCP keepalive, where it can
client_user = httpx.Client(base_url="http://YOUR_GPU:8000", transport=transport_user)

warm_user = window.Warm(ping=lambda: client_user.get("/ping"))     # a ping while the connection is idle
warm_user.used()                                              # call it each time you send on the connection
```

Run against the quickstart's server, those lines sent four pings in 0.45 seconds of idle time. One thing `connect()`
does that your own client must do itself: never let a ping and a request run at the same time. An HTTP/1.1 client
that starts a request while a ping is in flight opens a second connection for it, with a new handshake and a cold
window. `connect()` uses one connection and a lock; [`link.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/link.py) is short enough to read.

[`examples/components/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/examples/components) has a runnable file for each component, and
[Components](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/components.md) describes what each one does, what it needs and what was measured.

## Which components help on your link

A component saves time only on a link that has the cost it removes. Measure before you add:

| On your link | Add | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| A short round-trip time (round-trip time (RTT), about 21 ms) and pauses between requests | `connect()`, or `window` on your own client | 40 of 40 requests took one extra round trip without BBR, none with it |
| A longer RTT (about 101 or 241 ms), no loss | nothing for the pauses | 0 or 1 of 40 requests took an extra round trip with the default settings |
| A tunnel or proxy in front of the server | `one_write` | GET p50 189.7 ms with headers and body written apart, 106.7 ms in one write |
| Large raw arrays on a slow uplink | compression, on by default with `serve()` | 172,800-byte frames came out about 1.9 times smaller for 0.37 ms |
| A new connection for each call | keep one open, as `connect()` does | 305.9 ms per call with a new connection, 121.0 ms reusing one |

The conditions behind each row are in the [README](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#results).
[How do I measure the link between my robot and my GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md)
shows how to get the same numbers for your own link.

## Before a robot depends on it

- **A token.** `serve()` with no token runs the policy for anyone who can reach its port, and says so when it starts.
  Start it with `serve(policy, token="...")` (or set `SEQ_SERVE_TOKEN` on the GPU) and connect with
  `sequence_ai.connect(url, token="...")`; open the port only to your robot's address as well.
- **The first answer.** A model compiled on its first inference takes tens of seconds. `serve(example=...)` runs it
  before the server says it is ready, `link.wait_until_ready()` waits for that on the robot, and `connect()` gives the
  first act 120 s in any case.
- **Several robots on one GPU.** `serve(..., batch=[1, 2, 4, 8])`, above. One replica of a model per GPU:
  [How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md)
- **No GPU near the robot.** [How do I get a GPU near my robot?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md)

## See also

- [What is on by default, and how do I turn each part off?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/what-is-on-by-default.md)
- [Quickstart](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md)
- [FAQ](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/faq.md), for the errors a first run can print
- [Comparison with openpi's and LeRobot's remote inference](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/comparison.md)
